This division relates to the Policy _[For limiting availability of welfare payments](/policies/34)_. The majority voted against an amendment to the original motion, introduced by Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young. The original motion was "that the bill be now read a second time"(Read more about the stages that a bill must pass through to become law [here](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ) to which Senator Hanson-Young moved the following amendment: _At the end of the motion, add:_ _but the Senate is of the opinion that, rather than punishing families, revenue should be raised from big miners, bankers and polluters through:_ _(a) applying a 'public insurance' levy on the big four banks that are too big to fail;_ _(b) removing fossil fuel subsidised fuel for big mining companies;_ _(c) retaining the billions in revenue from the carbon price;_ _(d) implementing the original super profits mining tax;_ _(e) imposing a millionaires tax;_ _(f) taxing discretionary trusts as corporations; and_ _(g) imposing a levy on thermal coal imports exports._ Because the majority voted against this amendment, it was unsuccessful _Background to the bill_ The [bill](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5271) was introduced primarily to amend the [A New Tax System (Family Assistance) Act 1999](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsaa1999357/) in order to: - maintain the indexation pause on the [Child Care Rebate](http://www.humanservices.gov.au/customer/services/centrelink/child-care-rebate) (CCR) limit at $7500 for three years from 1 July 2014; and - maintain the [Child Care Benefit](http://www.humanservices.gov.au/customer/services/centrelink/child-care-benefit) (CCB) income thresholds at the amounts applicable as at 30 June 2014 for three years from 1 July 2014. Normally, the CCR limit and CCB income test thresholds are indexed on an annual basis to the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

Introduced the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014, freezing childcare benefit thresholds and the $7,500 rebate cap to save $230 million, and said an independent review found Labor's Early Years Quality Fund would have benefited less than 30 per cent of long day care workers before redirecting over $200 million to broader professional development.

Moved an amendment opposing the Child Care Measures Bill, arguing the government's paid parental leave scheme offers $50,000 cheques to millionaires while cutting childcare benefit for families earning as little as $42,000, and citing $230 million in cuts that the department says will affect around 500,000 families.

Argued the bill will strip $230 million from childcare benefit assistance relied on by over 889,000 families, said research shows every one per cent rise in childcare fees cuts mothers' workforce participation by 0.7 per cent, and noted 180 early childhood educators are leaving the underpaid sector every week.

Argued in support of the Child Care Measures Bill, detailing net savings of $105.8 million from freezing the childcare rebate and $230.4 million from freezing the childcare benefit, and said Labor had promised 260 new childcare centres but delivered only 38.

Defended the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014, which freezes the $7,500 childcare rebate limit and childcare benefit income thresholds for three years to save $230 million, saying childcare fees had risen 50 per cent nationally during Labor's six years in government.

Opposed the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014, saying it would strip $230 million from means-tested childcare benefits affecting 889,000 families, and that 74,000 families would reach the childcare rebate cut-off in 2014 alone.

Opposed the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014, saying it would cut $336 million from childcare support and leave over 500,000 families worse off, and cited a Grattan Institute study estimating Australia's economy could be $35 billion better off if it matched Canada's childcare-driven workforce participation.

Opposed the Family Assistance child care bill, citing Goodstart research that children who miss preschool are 50 per cent more likely to be developmentally vulnerable, and calculated the bill's $76.9 million saving is only about 1.5 per cent of what the government's Paid Parental Leave scheme would cost in a year.

Opposed the Family Assistance child care bill, citing Early Childhood Australia modelling that a family earning $60,000 with one child in care would be $1,800 a year worse off by 2016-17, and described the threat to Nikinpa Aboriginal Child and Family Centre in his Charlton electorate from a $78 million annual cut to Indigenous child and family centres.

Said the government is increasing overall childcare assistance to $28½ billion over four years for about a million families, defended maintaining childcare benefit thresholds and pausing the childcare rebate limit at $7,500 per child for three more years as a Labor-originated measure, and said childcare fees rose 53 per cent under the previous government.

This bill is one of a package that introduces a temporary budget repair levy for three years, starting in the 2014-15 financial year, as extra income tax on individuals.
The levy would be added to tax rates that are tied to the top personal marginal rate and to the Medicare levy, to keep the system fair and reduce avoidance.
The levy rate is two per cent of taxable income above $180,000, with no levy for income at or below that amount unless integrity rules apply.
Introduces a three-year temporary budget repair levy on individuals.
Aligns certain tax rates with the new levy to preserve fairness and prevent avoidance.
Ensures higher-income earners contribute more to budget repair.
Australian resident and foreign resident individuals with taxable income over $180,000.

Christine Milne I move: _At the end of the motion, add:_ _but the Senate calls on the government to:_ _(a) extend the provisions of the levy beyond the 2016-17 financial year, making the levy permanent; and_ _(b) guarantee that no tax cuts will be made, or promised, for the top income tax bracket, prior to the 2016 election._ In other words, no tax cut, or promise of one, is permitted before the 2016 election. That would test the mettle of this. If you are serious about a permanent change for those who earn more than $180,000, you would have no concerns at all about supporting this amendment. I call on both the government and the Labor Party to support this amendment. We are not going to let the government off the hook with their temporary levy. Criticized the budget's $30 billion cut to education and its plan to push people under 25 from Newstart onto the lower youth allowance, a cut of at least $48 a week or almost $2,500 a year, and warned nearly 600,000 Queensland pensioners' concessions are at risk from cuts to the states.

Argued this bill represents another broken promise on tax, cited NATSEM modelling that the poorest fifth of families with children will see a five per cent cut to disposable income against 0.3 per cent for the most affluent fifth, and recounted a distressed pensioner constituent with chronic leukaemia worried about affording her monthly medical treatment.

Detailed feedback from her Indi budget impact tour, said the levy will raise $3.1 billion by taxing the 2.3 per cent of Australians earning over $180,000, and moved an amendment to extend the levy to 2020 to 2021 so the burden is shared more fairly.

Criticised the budget's broken promises, said the government's $80 billion cut to education and health includes scrapping the Australia Network at a cost of $200 million to the ABC over eight years, and said changing the pension indexation method would leave a pensioner about $1,500 a year worse off had it applied over the past four years.

Argued the levy is necessary given the nation's $12 billion annual interest bill, equivalent to $1 billion a month, and warned that if unchecked, debt reaching $667 billion would push interest payments to $3 billion a month.

Defended the temporary budget repair levy raising the top marginal tax rate from 45 to 47 per cent on incomes above $180,000 from 1 July 2014 to 30 June 2017, noting that combined with other levies this would give Australia the world's eighth-highest marginal tax rate, compared with 33 per cent in New Zealand, 20 per cent in Singapore and 15 per cent in Hong Kong.

Argued that Labor would not block the Tax Laws Amendment (Temporary Budget Repair Levy) Bill 2014, but cited NATSEM modelling showing the poorest 20 per cent of families, earning less than $35,000 a year after tax, will lose almost five per cent of disposable income, versus a 0.2 per cent loss for the top 20 per cent earning $88,000 or more.

Argued against the broader budget package while not opposing the levy itself, said his Fowler electorate has an average personal income of about $20,000 and an average household income of $55,000, well below the $180,000 threshold at which the new levy applies.

Argued that the poorest bear the heaviest burden in this budget, citing modelling that a young jobseeker earning just over $13,000 a year will lose almost $7,000, and said about 30 per cent of her Bendigo electorate survives on less than $600 a week.

Explained that the Tax Laws Amendment (Temporary Budget Repair Levy) Bill 2014 introduces a three-year, two per cent levy on taxable income above $180,000, starting in the 2014 to 2015 financial year, and accused the Prime Minister of promising no new taxes before the election then introducing this levy afterward.

Argued that the Tax Laws Amendment (Temporary Budget Repair Levy) Bill 2014 exposes the Prime Minister's broken tax promises, quoting his pre-election pledges that there would be tax cuts without new taxes, no new tax collection without an election, and that personal income tax would be lower under a coalition government.
Tax Laws Amendment (Temporary Budget Repair Levy) Act 2014

Clean Energy Finance Corporation (Abolition) Bill 2013 [No. 2] - Second Reading - Read a second time

Moved a debate management motion to limit debate on the Clean Energy Finance Corporation (Abolition) Bill 2013 [No. 2] to conclude by noon, after the bill was earlier rejected by the Senate, saying the government wanted it passed by the House so it could return to the Senate within seven weeks.

Argued the government's alternative Direct Action policy would transfer $4 billion to $5 billion of taxpayer money to polluters every year without matching emissions targets, according to economists Ross Garnaut and Ken Henry, and said the Clean Energy Finance Corporation had already invested $590 million to leverage $1.8 billion in private investment, while renewable energy policy had grown household solar installations from about 7,400 to 1.1 million.

Supported the bill, saying abolishing the Clean Energy Finance Corporation would save more than $6 billion in borrowed money by 30 June 2017 and $350 million in interest costs, and accused Labor of hypocrisy for opposing the carbon tax repeal in the Senate while claiming publicly to oppose the tax.

Opposed the bill, saying the Clean Energy Finance Corporation had catalysed more than $1.55 billion in private investment from just $536 million committed, delivering a 3.9 million tonne reduction in carbon emissions, and cited University of New South Wales solar cell research the corporation could help commercialise.

Supported the bill, arguing it is unusual for government to operate banking-style investment services outside limited precedents like the Indigenous Land Corporation and Screen Australia, and said two-thirds of the corporation's claimed 3.88 million tonne emissions reduction came from the Taralga, Portland and Macarthur wind farms, which were already supported by the renewable energy target.

Opposed the bill, criticising the government for gagging debate on significant legislation despite its rhetoric about freedom, and argued the Senate committee's evidence and reasoning for rejecting the bill late last year deserved further consideration rather than a rushed vote.
The bill would remove the need to re-approve and re-register agricultural and veterinary chemicals under the Agvet Code.
It would delete end dates for approvals and allow registrations to be renewed without a final renewal, while also cutting red tape and improving regulator access to safety information.

The bill also amends the Agricultural and Veterinary Chemicals Legislation Amendment Act 2013, the Food Standards Australia New Zealand Act 1991, and the Collection Act, with no start date specified in the outline.
Removes requirements for re-approval and re-registration of agvet chemicals.
Reduces red tape by allowing less frequent registration renewals.
Improves the APVMA's ability to obtain safety information on marketed chemicals.
Obliges the APVMA to give eligible persons access to approval and registration information.
Manufacturers, importers, and users of agricultural and veterinary chemicals, as well as the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA).
Agricultural and Veterinary Chemicals Legislation Amendment (Removing Re-approval and Re-registration) Bill 2014 - Second Reading - Read a second time

Argued in support of the agvet chemicals bill, said Tasmania's total exports in 2011 to 2012 were worth $3.4 billion with agriculture representing 30 per cent, and said the state's growing dairy industry will need at least 70,000 more cows to meet processing capacity.

Said Labor will not oppose the agvet chemicals bill pending a Senate inquiry, noted there are about 11,700 agricultural and veterinary chemicals registered in Australia, and said the bill removes the mandatory re-registration cycle Labor introduced of seven years for high-risk chemicals and 15 years for low-risk ones.

Argued in support of the agvet chemicals bill's safeguards, described SPC Ardmona finding dangerously high lead levels in Chinese-imported canned peaches, and explained that Australia's food import testing rate drops from 100 per cent to 25 per cent, then to just 5 per cent of shipments after consecutive passes.

Raised concerns that removing mandatory re-registration could weaken a safety 'guardrail', noting that of the roughly 11,700 agvet chemicals in use, about 8,350 are agricultural chemicals with 2,230 containing active constituents that have mostly never been subject to modern safety testing.

Detailed the coalition's broader agriculture agenda alongside the agvet chemicals bill, said the new post-entry quarantine facility at Mickleham in Victoria will cost $379.9 million and cover 144 hectares, with construction due in two stages finishing in late 2015 and late 2018.

Detailed her Durack electorate's $3.5 billion agriculture and aquaculture production, described the Ord River irrigation scheme where only 14,000 of a planned 40,000 hectares are currently irrigated, and noted the government's $482 million commitment to upgrade the Great Northern and North West Coastal highways.

Argued in support of the bill, cited CropLife estimates that 68 per cent of Australian crop production depends on approved agvet chemicals, and compared the extended seven-year renewal period to New South Wales recently extending safe drivers' licence renewals to up to 10 years.

Detailed the budget's agricultural commitments including $104 million for a competitive research grants program and $8 million over four years to improve agvet chemical registration, and highlighted Sylvan Australia and Regal Mushrooms in her electorate, which together produce about 20 per cent of Australia's mushroom supply.

Argued in support of the bill, said Australia's gross farm production is worth an estimated $47.9 billion a year with export commodities worth around $38 billion, and cited CropLife Australia estimating that 68 per cent of the value of Australian crop production depends on crop protection products.

Supported the bill removing duplicate reapproval and re-registration requirements for agricultural and veterinary chemicals, said the change will save industry up to $9 million annually, and noted Australia's roughly 12,000 registered agvet chemicals support a primary production sector worth an estimated $30 billion a year.

Supported removing mandatory chemical re-registration, citing Deloitte Access Economics finding 68 per cent of crop production relies on agvet chemicals, and detailed how the regulator's cut of the dimethoate residue limit from 0.02 to 0.001 milligrams per kilogram blocked tomato exports from the Bowen-Gumlu region, which produces $100 million worth of capsicums and $124 million of tomatoes annually, to New Zealand.

Supported the deregulation bill, projected to save the agvet chemical industry $1.3 million a year, while separately criticizing the APVMA's move to ban the fruit-fly chemical fenthion, whose consultation period closes 22 August, warning Hills orchard growers may need four different chemicals to replace the single one they currently rely on.

Supported easing chemical re-registration rules, noting Australia ranks eighth in world wheat production at about 21 million tonnes, under three per cent of the global crop, meaning manufacturers may not bother re-registering chemicals here, and likened glyphosate, protected by patents for about 20 years, to a once-in-a-century breakthrough like penicillin that risks being overused.

Summed up the debate on behalf of the Agriculture Minister, noting the bill contributes to a $1 billion a year reduction in red and green tape and could save industry up to $9 million, and reported that of 22 submissions to a Senate inquiry, 20 supported removing mandatory re-registration.
Agricultural and Veterinary Chemicals Legislation Amendment (Removing Re-approval and Re-registration) Act 2014

Introduced a bill amending the Migration Act in response to recent Federal Court and High Court rulings, clarifying when a visa decision is finally determined, restoring a bar on repeat protection visa applications on different grounds, and reinstating a criterion requiring applicants not be assessed by ASIO as a security risk.

The Selection of Bills Committee presented its 11th report of 2013, recommending six bills be referred to specific committees for inquiry with set reporting dates, including the Environment Legislation Amendment Bill 2013 (report by 12 February 2014) and the Criminal Code Amendment (Harming Australians) Bill 2013 (report by 4 March 2014).

This bill aims to improve how registered organisations like unions and employer groups are run and overseen.
It would set up a new independent body called the Registered Organisations Commission with stronger investigation powers.
Penalties would rise and new criminal offences would apply for serious misconduct by officers, mirroring rules for company directors.
Establishes the Registered Organisations Commission as an independent regulator.
Strengthens financial reporting and transparency rules by making some obligations enforceable as civil remedy provisions.
Increases civil penalties and creates criminal offences for serious breaches of officers' duties.
Expands disclosure requirements for officers' material personal interests and changes grounds for disqualification from office.
Gives the Commissioner investigation and information-gathering powers modelled on those in the Australian Securities and Investments Commission Act 2001.
Registered organisations, their branches, and their officers.
Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 - Second Reading - Agree with bill's main idea
Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 - Second Reading - Agree to the bill's main idea

Introduced a bill establishing a Registered Organisations Commission modelled on the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, citing Craig Thomson facing more than 150 fraud related charges and Michael Williamson pleading guilty to misusing almost $1 million of Health Services Union funds, and raising maximum penalties from 60 penalty units to 1,200 for individuals and 6,000 for a body corporate.

Opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013, arguing the government has not proven current regulation is failing after Labor tripled penalties last year, and cited employer group submissions warning the bill imposes obligations more onerous than the Corporations Act 2001 requires of company directors.

Supported the bill, arguing the Health Services Union scandal involving Craig Thomson and Michael Williamson showed existing regulation of registered organisations is inadequate, and welcomed the new Registered Organisations Commission's stronger investigation and disclosure powers to prevent similar misconduct.

Opposed the bill, arguing that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Act 2012 already strengthened regulation and that unions differ fundamentally from for-profit corporations, cited the Australian Industry Group's view that the disclosure rules are unfair to non-profit organisations, and called for the bill to be referred to the Senate references committee.

Supported the bill, arguing that the Health Services Union scandal, which involved nearly $1 million of members' funds, shows the need for the new Registered Organisations Commission with stronger, ASIC-style investigation powers, and noted that Bill Shorten's own bill had been given only five days of Senate committee scrutiny.

Supported the bill, arguing it will reassure workers that their union contributions cannot be misappropriated after the Thomson affair and the Health Services Union scandal, and noted that Fair Work Australia's registered organisations include employer bodies such as the Australian Education Union, not only trade unions.

Opposed the bill, said the Independent Education Union raised fees by two per cent to meet compliance costs under similar legislation already introduced by Campbell Newman in Queensland, and objected that executive members would have to register even their young children's Dollarmite bank accounts as personal interests.

Supported the bill, arguing that unions and employer bodies control large sums, illustrated by a leadership contest for the Queensland branch of the Transport Workers Union that oversaw about $11 million in assets, with $500,000 reportedly spent to change its leadership, showing the need for stronger financial oversight.

A motion to refer the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 to the Education and Employment References Committee was proposed on behalf of Senator Wong but was blocked by an objection.

The motion to refer the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 to the Education and Employment References Committee was moved, arguing that the bill was rushed with only one day of public hearings and that further scrutiny was needed, while opponents cited the government's election mandate and the need for higher penalties for union officials, referencing Justice North's criticism of existing penalties and the support of figures like Paul Howes.

Opposed the Fair Work Registered Organisations Amendment Bill, noted the unusual alignment of both the Australian Industry Group and unions in calling for more time to consider it, and accused the government of failing Holden workers and axing a fund meant to raise early childhood educators' wages.

Opposed the bill, tracing the coalition's industrial relations approach back to the Howard government's 2004 Senate takeover and Work Choices, said Labor's 2012 reforms had already tripled penalties for union misconduct following the Health Services Union scandal, and noted the National Workplace Relations Consultative Council itself had recommended the bill be delayed for further consultation.

Opposed the bill and called for Senate committee referral, noted Labor's 2012 reforms had already tripled penalties for registered organisation misconduct, cited the Australian Industry Group's submission that its 78 unpaid councillors would face disclosure requirements exceeding those on well-paid company directors, and said some proposed penalties would increase by two-thirds or more beyond existing law.

Opposed the bill, said the current Fair Work registered organisations framework, introduced in 2009 and strengthened in 2012, already imposes tough penalties, criticised new criminal penalties of up to $340,000 or five years imprisonment as unnecessary duplication of existing law, and noted a government member mentioned unions 25 times in one speech despite denying the bill targeted them.
The speaker tabled additional information from inquiries into amendments to the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 and the effectiveness of NAPLAN.

The speaker moved a motion to change committee memberships, discharging Senator Urquhart and appointing Senator Gallacher to the National Disability Insurance Scheme Joint Standing Committee, and appointing substitute members for several other committees including Wright, Milne, and Ludlam.

Closed debate on the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013, citing HSU and other union slush fund scandals to justify establishing an independent Registered Organisations Commission with stronger investigative powers and higher civil and criminal penalties aligned with the Corporations Act, and noted the Senate Standing Committee on Education and Employment's report tabled on 2 December.

Opposed the bill reviving the Australian Building and Construction Commission, said the 2001 Cole royal commission cost $66 million over 18 months without producing a single criminal conviction, criticised the bill for denying workers the right to silence and legal representation in secret interviews, and noted a former Federal Court judge had previously described the consulting firm's productivity modelling underpinning the bill as deeply flawed.
Higher Education Support Amendment (Further Streamlining and Other Measures) Bill 2013

Three bills—the Australian Capital Territory (Self-Government) Amendment Bill 2013, the Higher Education Support Amendment (Further Streamlining and Other Measures) Bill 2013, and the Royal Commissions Amendment Bill 2013—were introduced together, with a motion to proceed without formalities and be read a first time agreed to.
